column1: In Airflow, what is the difference between a DAG and a DAG Run?
column2: A DAG is the definition (the recipe) — a description that can never fail. A DAG Run is one actual execution of it for one data interval. States (success/failed/queued) belong to DAG Runs and Task Instances, never to the DAG or Task.

column1: With LocalExecutor, which process actually executes your task code, and are there worker pods?
column2: The scheduler itself — LocalExecutor forks task subprocesses inside the scheduler pod. There are no worker pods, so task memory comes out of the scheduler's limit and a fat task can OOM-kill the whole orchestrator.

column1: Does the Airflow 2 webserver parse DAG files?
column2: No. It renders the UI entirely from the serialized_dag table in the metadata DB. In this lab the DAG files are not even mounted into the webserver pod.

column1: How can the scheduler schedule a PythonOperator task without being able to run its function?
column2: Serialization stores structure only. A BashOperator's bash_command is a string and serializes; a Python callable cannot be serialized, so the scheduler knows the task exists but not its code. The task subprocess imports the DAG file to get the real function.

min_file_process_interval (30s default here) = how often an already-known DAG file is re-parsed. dag_dir_list_interval (300s) = how often the folder is rescanned for new or removed files. A brand-new DAG can lag by minutes; airflow dags reserialize forces it.

column1: Why must no real work (queries, API calls, file reads) live at module level in a DAG file?
column2: Module-level code runs on every parse — every ~30s per file, forever, even while the DAG is paused — AND once more in each task subprocess, which re-imports the module to reach the callable.

column1: For a scheduled @daily DAG, when does the run for Monday's data actually start, and why?
column2: Just after midnight on Tuesday — at the END of its data interval. A day's data cannot be processed until the day is over.

column1: What is logical_date, and why was its old name execution_date misleading?
column2: It is the run's identity, equal to data_interval_start for scheduled runs. It is NOT the time of execution: the run for Monday has logical_date Monday but executes on Tuesday.

column1: When do ds and data_interval_start disagree?
column2: On a manual trigger. logical_date (and therefore ds) becomes "now", while data_interval stays the last complete interval. Triggering at 05:26 on Aug 27 gave ds=2026-08-27 but data_interval=[2026-08-26, 2026-08-27).

column1: Which template variables should window a query, and why never ds?
column2: data_interval_start / data_interval_end. They agree with ds on a schedule but diverge on a manual run — exactly when someone is re-running a failed day — so WHERE order_date = '{{ ds }}' silently pulls the wrong day.

column1: Name three normal Airflow features that guarantee a task will run more than once.
column2: Retries after a transient failure, clearing a Task Instance in the UI, and backfill. All three re-execute code that already partly ran, which is why idempotency is mandatory.

column1: Why is a plain INSERT never idempotent, and what are two ClickHouse fixes?
column2: Each re-run appends duplicates silently: 1 row, then 2 after a retry, then 3 after a clear, with no error. Fix by DROP PARTITION for the interval before inserting, or by loading into ReplacingMergeTree(version) so the newest row per key wins.
